title: Rajma masala
summary: Kidney beans in a slow-built onion-tomato base. Mostly hands-off in a pressure cooker, and a bowl gives you 15 g of protein and 13 g of fibre.

time.note: Plus overnight soaking, or use tinned beans and skip to step 3.

ingredients.qty: 1.5 cups dry, soaked overnight - or 2 tins, drained

steps: Drain the soaked beans, cover with fresh water in the pressure cooker, add 1/2 tsp salt and a bay leaf. Cook 5-6 whistles, then let the pressure drop on its own. A cooked rajma should squash completely between two fingers - undercooked kidney beans are the main way this dish goes wrong.
Keep the cooking water. That starchy liquid is what thickens the gravy.

In a pan, heat the oil and crackle the cumin. Add the onions and cook them for a full 8-10 minutes to deep golden brown. This is the single biggest lever on how good the final dish tastes - do not rush it.
Ginger-garlic paste for 90 seconds, then the powdered spices with a splash of water.
Pour in the tomato puree. Cook 8-10 minutes until it darkens, thickens, and the oil beads out at the edges.
Add the beans with about 1.5 cups of their cooking liquid and the rest of the salt. Simmer 15 minutes, uncovered.
Mash roughly a quarter of the beans against the side of the pan with a ladle - this is what makes the gravy thick and creamy without any cream.
Finish with garam masala, crushed kasuri methi and coriander. It tastes better the next day.
tips: Never salt beans heavily before they are soft - the skins toughen and they stop absorbing water.
Tinned beans: skip step 1, use vegetable stock in place of the bean water, simmer 10 minutes.
The soaking water is what causes most of the digestive trouble. Throw it away and cook in fresh water.
health_notes: 13 g of fibre a serving, and the resistant starch in cooked-then-cooled beans is genuinely good for gut bacteria. Leftovers reheated the next day are better for you, not worse.

source.adapted: Punjabi home rajma with the ghee cut back and no cream in the finish.
